guide.title: Clinical Decision Making
guide.lead: Good clinicians make a working diagnosis early, then try to prove it wrong. Gather the facts, think of the worst it could be, act, reassess, and change your mind when the evidence changes. Know the traps your brain sets.

steps.title: Gather
steps.text: Scene, history, exam, vital signs, monitors.

steps.title: Revise
steps.text: Change the impression when the evidence changes.

sections.title: Thinking traps
rows: Look for findings that don't fit
Stopping once you have an answer
Thinking of what you saw recently

groups.title: Injury
items: Penetrating injury to head, neck, torso or proximal limbs
Skull deformity; chest wall instability; suspected pelvic fracture
Crushed, mangled or pulseless limb; amputation above the wrist or ankle
Bleeding needing a tourniquet or packing

groups.title: Mental status
items: Unable to follow commands (motor GCS below 6)

groups.title: Circulation (adult)
items: Heart rate greater than systolic BP

groups.title: Moderate risk (yellow) includes
items: Falls over 10 feet (3 m); high-risk crashes
Age 65 or older, or anticoagulation, with significant injury

groups.title: Deviating from protocol
items: What the protocol said, why you deviated, what you did
Who authorised it (medical direction) and the outcome

quiz.q: The nurse says "another UTI", but you find unequal pupils and one-sided weakness. Accepting her label would be:
quiz.explanation: Assess for yourself: this may be a stroke or bleed.

quiz.q: You decide "heart failure" and ignore unilateral leg swelling and a recent long flight. Which bias?
quiz.explanation: PE should be on the list.

quiz.q: Most important when documenting a protocol deviation:
options: Medical direction contact and the orders received (or why contact wasn't possible)
quiz.explanation: Plus what you did and the outcome.

options: A working diagnosis that guides treatment and changes with new evidence
Follow the first protocol you think of

quiz.q: Stopping your assessment once you think you know the answer:

options: Voice a safety concern twice, then escalate

quiz.q: Which is a high-risk (red) trauma triage criterion?
options: Heart rate greater than systolic BP in an adult

quiz.q: Fall from 12 feet, alert and stable. Field triage?
options: Moderate-risk mechanism: a trauma centre per protocol

quiz.q: Worst-first thinking for chest pain means:
options: Treat as ACS until proven otherwise

flashcards.question: Field impression vs diagnosis
flashcards.answer: A field impression is your working diagnosis that guides treatment and transport; it changes as evidence comes in.

flashcards.question: Reasoning cycle
flashcards.answer: Gather → interpret → field impression → act → reassess → revise.

flashcards.question: Documenting a protocol deviation
flashcards.answer: What the protocol said, why you deviated, what you did, who authorised it, and the outcome.

flashcards.question: Anchoring
flashcards.answer: Locking onto the first impression and ignoring contrary evidence. Counter: build a differential and look for what doesn't fit.

flashcards.question: Worst-case thinking
flashcards.answer: Ask "What's the worst this could be?" and manage for it while you work it out.

flashcards.question: Two-challenge rule
flashcards.answer: Voice a safety concern twice; if unresolved, escalate to a supervisor or medical direction.

flashcards.question: Premature closure
flashcards.answer: Stopping the assessment once you have an answer: you miss findings that contradict it.

flashcards.question: Protocol vs field impression
flashcards.answer: A protocol is the approved treatment guide; your field impression decides which protocol applies.

critical.scenario: A 52-year-old is gasping: tripoding, one-word answers, RR 36, SpO₂ 82%, HR 112. Clear lungs, no JVD, no edema, no fever. He had knee surgery 10 days ago and has been mostly immobile.
critical.question: Field impression and plan?

options.t: Possible pulmonary embolism: oxygen to target, position of comfort, rapid transport and pre-alert, watch for collapse

options.f: No wheeze; risk factors point to PE.

critical.explanation: Sudden breathlessness with clear lungs and hypoxia plus recent surgery is PE until proven otherwise.

critical.scenario: A worker fell 12 feet onto his feet: severe low back pain, both heels deformed, alert, stable vital signs. Trauma centre 35 minutes; community hospital 12 minutes. The foreman asks why not the closer hospital.
critical.question: Destination and explanation?

options.t: Trauma centre: a fall over 10 feet with a heel-and-spine (axial load) pattern can hide spinal fractures and bleeding

options.f: The mechanism and injury pattern point to the trauma centre.

options.t: Let him choose by walking to the ambulance

critical.explanation: Field triage 2021 lists falls over 10 feet (3 m) as a moderate-risk mechanism.

critical.scenario: A 74-year-old has crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm for 45 minutes. BP 98/66, HR 92, SpO₂ 94%. Your protocol allows nitroglycerin only with systolic above 100 mmHg.
critical.question: Best course?

options.t: Hold nitroglycerin per protocol, aspirin, 12-lead now and transmit, no oxygen (SpO₂ above 90%), contact medical direction, frequent BP checks

options.f: Protocol limits exist for good reason, especially in RV infarction.

options.t: High-flow oxygen and leave the 12-lead to the hospital
No aspirin because of the low BP

critical.explanation: Document that nitroglycerin was held and why.
